briefOverview: Sarai gives her slave Hagar to Abram to bear a child, leading to jealousy, Hagar’s flight, and a divine encounter that promises many descendants through Hagar’s son Ishmael.
summary: Sarai, barren after ten years in Canaan, gives her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abram as a surrogate; Hagar conceives and treats Sarai with contempt. Sarai blames Abram, who leaves the disciplining to her; Hagar flees. The angel of the LORD finds Hagar at a spring, instructs her to return and submit, announces she will bear a son named Ishmael, and promises his offspring will be numerous. Hagar calls the Lord who spoke to her "God sees me," the well is named Beer-lahai-roi, and Hagar bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.
externalContext: In the ancient Near East it was an accepted practice for a barren wife to give a slave or maidservant to her husband to bear children (a form of surrogacy or concubinage), and slave women occupied ambiguous social and legal positions within households. Wells and springs were vital lifelines in nomadic and semi-nomadic contexts and often mark the scenes of important encounters. The figure called the "angel of the LORD" in Genesis often functions as a divine messenger or theophany, carrying authoritative promises about offspring and destiny.
externalReferences: This episode anticipates and connects with Genesis 17, where God establishes the covenant with Abram (renaming him Abraham) and promises a son (Isaac) through Sarah, clarifying the covenant line. Genesis 21 records the later birth of Isaac and the eventual sending away of Hagar and Ishmael (Genesis 21:8–21), showing how the tension begun here continues. Genesis 25:12–18 lists Ishmael’s descendants, fulfilling the promise that Ishmael would become a great nation. Genesis 15 (God’s promise of offspring) provides the broader narrative background for concerns about Abraham’s seed.
practicalQuestions: How should communities today address the ethical implications when vulnerable people are used to achieve others' goals?
In situations of household or workplace jealousy, what constructive steps can be taken to protect those with less power?
How do we recognize and respond to moments when marginalized people experience care or affirmation?
When human plans cause harm, how can we seek reconciliation that acknowledges both agency and accountability?
uncertainAreas: The precise theological status of the "angel of the LORD" (pure messenger, theophany, or divine presence) is open to interpretation, and the text leaves ambiguous legal/social details about Hagar’s status (wife, concubine, or slave). The characterization of Ishmael as a "wild man" is descriptive but vague in its long-term implications and invites differing readings about his future role.
